9ab712e3b6c233ce697acea32b657c1ae2fceefd.label: Bell tent
9ab712e3b6c233ce697acea32b657c1ae2fceefd.note: Built in the asset box: the Things’ bell tent, pitched, and its fire place lit in front of its door; walked in by its own shape, pitched again, the fire lit or put out

af92cc91b8faec9c96d504aabf723f344d2e216e.label: BatteryCube: BatteryCube
af92cc91b8faec9c96d504aabf723f344d2e216e.note: as at v1: busbars down the front, a one-way inverter

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, and the copper busbars that join them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW hybrid inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input, gives 230 V to the sockets, and takes a charge from an ElectroCube or the grid when the sun is short.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Tray
parts.what: The pack’s aluminium tray: a floor and four walls the holders sit in, with ribs under it to slide on rails.

parts.label: Front panel
parts.what: The pack’s face: it closes the tray’s front and carries the handles, the terminals and the state-of-charge lights.

parts.label: Handles
parts.what: Two handles on its face to slide it in and out: at ~26 kg one person lifts it.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Terminals
parts.what: The pack’s plus and minus on its face, under their covers, and the data plug for the BMS beside them.

parts.label: Lid
parts.what: The aluminium lid and the spring pad under it: closing it presses every contact plate onto its poles, the whole pack’s only joining force.

parts.label: Latches
parts.what: Four over-centre latches, two a side: flip them and the lid lifts. No tool opens the pack.

2e187ade50c210ad2f354ec452703afbccf5015e.label: BatteryCube: BatteryCube
2e187ade50c210ad2f354ec452703afbccf5015e.note: ~20.7 kWh, 6 kW at 230 V both ways, an MPPT solar input, an AC inlet, 686 × 660 × 686 mm, ~140 kg

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, each plugged by its back into the backplane that joins them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW bidirectional inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input or from outside power at its AC inlet (the grid, an ElectroCube, a generator), and gives 230 V to the sockets.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Shell
parts.what: The pack’s outer shell: a foot (its floor tub and, across the face, a sill), walls, top and back in one smooth aluminium piece, open at the front above the sill where the service drawer slides in. It is what you carry and what the cube holds: the grip, the ClickLock and the two release buttons are all on it, in the sill.

parts.label: Front plate
parts.what: The upright of the service drawer’s L: the pack’s face above the sill, its round front corners and bands flush with the shell. A long finger pull along its foot and the charge strip along its top; nothing you carry by. The base plate is fixed to its foot.

parts.label: Base plate
parts.what: The floor of the service drawer’s L, riding on the shell’s foot: every inner part is mounted on it, the cells’ holders, the contact plates, the clamp and the BMS. It runs on two low-friction strips and slides out over the sill.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Grip
parts.what: One grip for one hand on the shell itself, in the middle of the sill across its foot: carry the pack by it and the shell takes the weight, never the drawer. Its trigger sits at the very height of the ClickLock’s pawls in the foot, so the two release cables run straight to them: close your fingers round it and the pawls pull back, so the pack slides out in the same move; let go and it clicks home again.
specs: Bar 10 mm over the foot, trigger at 10 mm: the lock’s height

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Back socket
parts.what: The pack’s plus, minus and data in one socket flush in its back, nothing sticking out. Its contacts sit at the bottom of pockets that take the cube’s insulating collars: the collars slide in first, then the pins meet their contacts, so no metal is ever open to a finger on either side. Two lined guide holes take the cube’s guide pins first: slide the pack in and it plugs itself into the backplane; pull it out and it lets go.
specs: 2 pockets ⌀ 19 mm, sockets for ⌀ 8 mm pins, 120 A [inferred]
2 lined holes, ⌀ 11 mm, for ⌀ 10 mm pins

parts.label: Pawls
parts.what: Two steel levers, one inside each side wall. Each pivots at its back end; its tooth at the front pokes out through a slot in the wall. Sliding in, the tooth rides up the rail’s ramp, is pushed in, and snaps out again behind the keeper: that is the click.

parts.label: Pawl springs
parts.what: A small coil spring behind each pawl presses its tooth outward, so it always drops into the keeper on its own: you never have to lock it, only to unlock it.

parts.label: Pivot pins
parts.what: A pin through each pawl’s back end, standing in the case floor: the pawl swings round it, in and out.

parts.label: Release cables
parts.what: Two short steel cables in sleeves, both at the pawls’ own height: from the trigger in through the face, along its inside to the corner and straight back along the side wall to the pawl, no bend up or down. Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Trigger
parts.what: The bar under the grip: your fingers close round the grip and press it up, it pulls both cables, and the pawls let go. Let go and the springs push it back.

parts.label: Clamp
parts.what: A stiff plate on four posts over the cells, its spring pad pressing every top contact plate onto its poles: the job the lid did, now on the drawer, so the cells stay pressed when it comes out.

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug that slides onto the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home.

parts.label: Release button, left
parts.what: A round push button in the face of the shell’s corner column on its side, at the base plate’s level: part of the shell, so it stays put while the drawer comes out. Behind it a short plunger with a wedge runs back inside the column and pushes the catch’s bolt out of its notch in the base plate. Press both, pull the drawer by its finger pull, and the whole inside slides out between the columns.

parts.label: Drawer catch, left
parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.

Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Trigger
parts.what: The bar under the grip: your fingers close round the grip and press it up, it pulls both cables, and the pawls let go. Let go and the springs push it back.

parts.label: Clamp
parts.what: A stiff plate on four posts over the cells, its spring pad pressing every top contact plate onto its poles: the job the lid did, now on the drawer, so the cells stay pressed when it comes out.

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug that slides onto the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home.

parts.label: Release button, left
parts.what: A round push button in the face of the shell’s corner column on its side, at the base plate’s level: part of the shell, so it stays put while the drawer comes out. Behind it a short plunger with a wedge runs back inside the column and pushes the catch’s bolt out of its notch in the base plate. Press both, pull the drawer by its finger pull, and the whole inside slides out between the columns.

parts.label: Drawer catch, left
parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.

parts.label: Release button, right
parts.what: A round push button in the face of the shell’s corner column on its side, at the base plate’s level: part of the shell, so it stays put while the drawer comes out. Behind it a short plunger with a wedge runs back inside the column and pushes the catch’s bolt out of its notch in the base plate. Press both, pull the drawer by its finger pull, and the whole inside slides out between the columns.

parts.label: Drawer catch, right
parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.

parts.label: Backplane
parts.what: A board behind the stack with a pin header for each BatteryPack. Every live pin stands sunk in its own insulating collar: the two copper power pins each in a round shroud, the four data pins together in one between them, their tips 5 mm below the rims, so a finger (or a dropped tool) meets plastic, never metal (finger-safe, IP2X). Slide a pack in and the collars go into matching pockets in its back socket before any pin touches its contact. Two long steel guide pins with pointed tips find the pack’s guide holes first; they carry no current, so they stay bare. Copper bars inside the board join the four side by side and carry their 52 V to the inverter.
specs: 2 per pack, ⌀ 8 mm, 120 A [inferred], each in a ⌀ 18 mm collar, 5 mm sunk
4 per pack, CAN, in one shroud, 5 mm sunk
2 per pack, ⌀ 10 × 24 mm, pointed, no current

parts.label: Pack rails
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. Here: a pair of rails for each BatteryPack, their keepers where the pack’s back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Hybrid inverter
parts.what: One bidirectional box does it all: an MPPT solar charger, a charger from outside power and a pure-sine inverter. It fills the packs from the panels by day, or from the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator at its AC inlet, and turns their 52 V into 230 V for the home.

parts.label: Solar input
parts.what: Where the panels plug in: a pair of MC4 connectors, plus and minus, and the DC isolator that cuts them off.

parts.label: AC inlet
parts.what: Where outside power comes in to charge it: a red-ringed 230 V inlet under a spring lid. Plug in the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator and the inverter runs backwards, filling the packs.

parts.label: Sockets and breakers
parts.what: What it gives out: two blue 230 V sockets under spring lids for a home or tools, behind a main breaker and a 30 mA earth-leakage breaker.

steps: Cut, drill and bolt the frame: skids, posts, top rails, quick-attach plate
Fit the backplane; slide in the four BatteryPacks, each plugs itself in
Mount the inverter on the back; wire the solar input, the AC inlet, the breakers and the sockets

ff78e8976c0e3862db236d3aa4079fb820006270.label: BatteryCube: BatteryCube
ff78e8976c0e3862db236d3aa4079fb820006270.note: as at v2: a one-way inverter

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, each plugged by its back into the backplane that joins them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW bidirectional inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input or from outside power at its AC inlet (the grid, an ElectroCube, a generator), and gives 230 V to the sockets.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Case
parts.what: The pack’s case: one smooth aluminium shell with round corners, its floor and four walls, a darker foot band, and rails under it to slide on.

parts.label: Front panel
parts.what: The pack’s face, set into the case’s front: it carries the handles, the charge strip along its top; its power and data leave by the plug in its back.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Handles
parts.what: Two handles on its face to slide it in and out: at ~26 kg one person lifts it.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Back plug
parts.what: The pack’s plus, minus and data in one blind-mate plug in its back, between two guide pins: slide the pack in and it plugs itself into the cube’s backplane; pull it out by its handles and it lets go. No cables, no bolts.

parts.label: ClickLock
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. In a BatteryCube the pawls click in just as its back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Lid
parts.what: The lid, its round corners and soft edge flush with the case, and the spring pad under it: closing it presses every contact plate onto its poles, the whole pack’s only joining force.

parts.label: Latches
parts.what: Four flush over-centre latches, two a side: flip them and the lid lifts. No tool opens the pack.

parts.label: Top contact plates

parts.label: Battery management system

parts.label: Back plug

parts.label: ClickLock
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. In a BatteryCube the pawls click in just as its back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Lid
parts.what: The lid, its round corners and soft edge flush with the case, and the spring pad under it: closing it presses every contact plate onto its poles, the whole pack’s only joining force.

parts.label: Latches

parts.label: Backplane

parts.label: Case
parts.what: The pack’s case: one smooth aluminium shell with round corners, its floor and four walls, a darker foot band, and rails under it to slide on.

parts.label: Front panel
parts.what: The pack’s face, set into the case’s front: it carries the handles, the charge strip along its top; its power and data leave by the plug in its back.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Grip
parts.what: One grip in the middle of its face, for one hand: close your fingers round it and its trigger pulls the ClickLock’s pawls back, so the pack slides out in the same move; let go and it clicks home again. The pack hangs balanced under it.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates

parts.label: Pawls
parts.what: Two steel levers, one inside each side wall. Each pivots at its back end; its tooth at the front pokes out through a slot in the wall. Sliding in, the tooth rides up the rail’s ramp, is pushed in, and snaps out again behind the keeper: that is the click.

parts.label: Pawl springs
parts.what: A small coil spring behind each pawl presses its tooth outward, so it always drops into the keeper on its own: you never have to lock it, only to unlock it.

parts.label: Pivot pins
parts.what: A pin through each pawl’s back end, standing in the case floor: the pawl swings round it, in and out.

parts.label: Release cables
parts.what: Two short steel cables in sleeves run from the trigger along the inside of the face to the two pawls. Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Solar input

parts.label: AC inlet

parts.label: Sockets and breakers

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, each plugged by its back into the backplane that joins them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW bidirectional inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input or from outside power at its AC inlet (the grid, an ElectroCube, a generator), and gives 230 V to the sockets.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Grip

Close your fingers round it and the trigger pulls both pawls back, so the pack slides out in the same move; let go and it clicks home again.

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, each plugged by its back into the backplane that joins them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW bidirectional inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input or from outside power at its AC inlet (the grid, an ElectroCube, a generator), and gives 230 V to the sockets.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Shell
parts.what: The pack’s outer shell: floor, walls, top and back in one smooth aluminium piece with round corners, open only at the front where the service drawer slides in. No lid and no latches any more: nothing opens but the drawer.

parts.label: Front plate
parts.what: The upright of the service drawer’s L: the pack’s whole face, its round front corners and bands flush with the shell. It carries the grip, the charge strip and the ClickLock; the base plate is fixed to its foot.

parts.label: Base plate
parts.what: The floor of the service drawer’s L: every inner part is mounted on it, the cells’ holders, the contact plates, the clamp and the BMS. It runs on the shell’s floor on two low-friction strips.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Grip
parts.what: One grip for one hand, low on its face near the case’s foot: its trigger sits at the very height of the ClickLock’s pawls, so the two release cables run straight to them. Close your fingers round it and the trigger pulls both pawls back, so the pack slides out in the same move; let go and it clicks home again.
specs: Bar 40 mm over the foot, trigger at 30 mm: the lock’s height

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Back socket
parts.what: The pack’s plus, minus and data in one socket flush in its back: proper holes, nothing sticking out. Two lined guide holes take the cube’s guide pins first, then its two power pins and four data pins slide into their sockets: slide the pack in and it plugs itself into the backplane; pull it out and it lets go. With nothing proud on its back, it stands on any shelf and no contact gets bent.
specs: 2 lined holes, ⌀ 11 mm, for ⌀ 10 mm pins

parts.label: Pawls
parts.what: Two steel levers, one inside each side wall. Each pivots at its back end; its tooth at the front pokes out through a slot in the wall. Sliding in, the tooth rides up the rail’s ramp, is pushed in, and snaps out again behind the keeper: that is the click.

parts.label: Pawl springs
parts.what: A small coil spring behind each pawl presses its tooth outward, so it always drops into the keeper on its own: you never have to lock it, only to unlock it.

parts.label: Pivot pins
parts.what: A pin through each pawl’s back end, standing in the case floor: the pawl swings round it, in and out.

parts.label: Release cables
parts.what: Two short steel cables in sleeves, both at the pawls’ own height: from the trigger in through the face, along its inside to the corner and straight back along the side wall to the pawl, no bend up or down. Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Trigger

parts.label: Clamp

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug that slides onto the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home.

parts.label: Release button, left

parts.label: Backplane
parts.what: A board behind the stack with a pin header for each BatteryPack: two long steel guide pins with pointed tips find the pack’s guide holes first, then two copper power pins and four data pins slide into its sockets. The pins are on the cube, the holes in the pack: a pack on its own has nothing sticking out. Copper bars inside the board join the four side by side and carry their 52 V to the inverter.

parts.label: Pack rails
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. Here: a pair of rails for each BatteryPack, their keepers where the pack’s back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Hybrid inverter
parts.what: One bidirectional box does it all: an MPPT solar charger, a charger from outside power and a pure-sine inverter. It fills the packs from the panels by day, or from the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator at its AC inlet, and turns their 52 V into 230 V for the home.

parts.label: Solar input
parts.what: Where the panels plug in: a pair of MC4 connectors, plus and minus, and the DC isolator that cuts them off.

parts.label: AC inlet
parts.what: Where outside power comes in to charge it: a red-ringed 230 V inlet under a spring lid. Plug in the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator and the inverter runs backwards, filling the packs.

parts.label: Sockets and breakers
parts.what: What it gives out: two blue 230 V sockets under spring lids for a home or tools, behind a main breaker and a 30 mA earth-leakage breaker.

parts.label: Pawls

parts.label: Backplane
parts.what: A board behind the stack with a pin header for each BatteryPack. Every live pin stands sunk in its own insulating collar: the two copper power pins each in a round shroud, the four data pins together in one between them, their tips 5 mm below the rims, so a finger (or a dropped tool) meets plastic, never metal (finger-safe, IP2X). Slide a pack in and the collars go into matching pockets in its back socket before any pin touches its contact. Two long steel guide pins with pointed tips find the pack’s guide holes first; they carry no current, so they stay bare. Copper bars inside the board join the four side by side and carry their 52 V to the inverter.
specs: 2 per pack, ⌀ 8 mm, 120 A [inferred], each in a ⌀ 18 mm collar, 5 mm sunk
4 per pack, CAN, in one shroud, 5 mm sunk
2 per pack, ⌀ 10 × 24 mm, pointed, no current

parts.label: Pack rails
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. Here: a pair of rails for each BatteryPack, their keepers where the pack’s back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Hybrid inverter
parts.what: One bidirectional box does it all: an MPPT solar charger, a charger from outside power and a pure-sine inverter. It fills the packs from the panels by day, or from the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator at its AC inlet, and turns their 52 V into 230 V for the home.

parts.label: Solar input
parts.what: Where the panels plug in: a pair of MC4 connectors, plus and minus, and the DC isolator that cuts them off.

parts.label: AC inlet
parts.what: Where outside power comes in to charge it: a red-ringed 230 V inlet under a spring lid. Plug in the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator and the inverter runs backwards, filling the packs.

parts.label: Sockets and breakers
parts.what: What it gives out: two blue 230 V sockets under spring lids for a home or tools, behind a main breaker and a 30 mA earth-leakage breaker.

steps: Cut, drill and bolt the frame: skids, posts, top rails, quick-attach plate
Fit the backplane; slide in the four BatteryPacks, each plugs itself in
Mount the inverter on the back; wire the solar input, the AC inlet, the breakers and the sockets

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: The Power Cube’s own 27" frame: two 4×4 tube skids, 2×2 angle posts and top rails, the quick-attach plate and two lifting eyes, so the BatteryCube is lifted, stacked and coupled like any cube.

assemblies.label: Battery
assemblies.note: Four BatteryPacks of 280 cells each (51.8 V, ~5.2 kWh), ~20.7 kWh in all, each plugged by its back into the backplane that joins them side by side.

assemblies.label: Inverter and sockets
assemblies.note: The 6 kW bidirectional inverter on the back: it charges the packs from the sun through its MPPT input or from outside power at its AC inlet (the grid, an ElectroCube, a generator), and gives 230 V to the sockets.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Shell
parts.what: The pack’s outer shell: a foot (its floor tub and, across the face, a sill), walls, top and back in one smooth aluminium piece, open at the front above the sill where the service drawer slides in. It is what you carry and what the cube holds: the grip, the ClickLock and the two release buttons are all on it, in the sill.

parts.label: Front plate
parts.what: The upright of the service drawer’s L: the pack’s face above the sill, its round front corners and bands flush with the shell. A long finger pull along its foot and the charge strip along its top; nothing you carry by. The base plate is fixed to its foot.

parts.label: Base plate

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Grip

Its trigger sits at the very height of the ClickLock’s pawls in the foot, so the two release cables run straight to them: close your fingers round it and the pawls pull back, so the pack slides out in the same move; let go and it clicks home again.

parts.label: Backplane
parts.what: A board behind the stack with a pin header for each BatteryPack. Every live pin stands sunk in its own insulating collar: the two copper power pins each in a round shroud, the four data pins together in one between them, their tips 5 mm below the rims, so a finger (or a dropped tool) meets plastic, never metal (finger-safe, IP2X). Slide a pack in and the collars go into matching pockets in its back socket before any pin touches its contact. Two long steel guide pins with pointed tips find the pack’s guide holes first; they carry no current, so they stay bare. Copper bars inside the board join the four side by side and carry their 52 V to the inverter.
specs: 2 per pack, ⌀ 8 mm, 120 A [inferred], each in a ⌀ 18 mm collar, 5 mm sunk
4 per pack, CAN, in one shroud, 5 mm sunk
2 per pack, ⌀ 10 × 24 mm, pointed, no current

parts.label: Pack rails
parts.what: Our one snap-in latch: slide it in and two spring pawls click into the keepers on the rails; press the flush tab on its face and both let go, and it slides out. No tool, no screw. Here: a pair of rails for each BatteryPack, their keepers where the pack’s back plug meets the backplane.

parts.label: Hybrid inverter
parts.what: One bidirectional box does it all: an MPPT solar charger, a charger from outside power and a pure-sine inverter. It fills the packs from the panels by day, or from the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator at its AC inlet, and turns their 52 V into 230 V for the home.

parts.label: Solar input
parts.what: Where the panels plug in: a pair of MC4 connectors, plus and minus, and the DC isolator that cuts them off.

parts.label: AC inlet
parts.what: Where outside power comes in to charge it: a red-ringed 230 V inlet under a spring lid. Plug in the grid, an ElectroCube or a generator and the inverter runs backwards, filling the packs.

parts.label: Sockets and breakers
parts.what: What it gives out: two blue 230 V sockets under spring lids for a home or tools, behind a main breaker and a 30 mA earth-leakage breaker.

steps: Cut, drill and bolt the frame: skids, posts, top rails, quick-attach plate
Fit the backplane; slide in the four BatteryPacks, each plugs itself in
Mount the inverter on the back; wire the solar input, the AC inlet, the breakers and the sockets

parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.
parts.moves: Sideways, 5 mm, out of its notch.
parts.drive: Its spring; the button’s wedge against it

parts.label: Pawls
parts.what: Two steel levers, one inside each side of the hollow foot. Each pivots at its back end; its tooth at the front pokes out through a slot in the wall. Sliding in, the tooth rides up the rail’s ramp, is pushed in, and snaps out again behind the keeper: that is the click.
parts.moves: Swing in 4 mm at the tooth when the trigger is pulled.
parts.drive: The release cables; the springs push them out again

parts.label: Pawl springs
parts.what: A small coil spring behind each pawl, against a boss on the floor, presses its tooth outward, so it always drops into the keeper on its own: you never have to lock it, only to unlock it.

parts.label: Pivot pins
parts.what: A pin through each pawl’s back end, standing between the foot’s two sheets: the pawl swings round it, in and out.

parts.label: Release cables
parts.what: Two short steel cables in sleeves, both at the pawls’ own height: from the trigger in through the face, along the inside of the hollow sill to the corner and straight back along the side of the foot to the pawl, no bend up or down. Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Trigger
parts.what: The bar under the grip: your fingers close round the grip and press it up, it pulls both cables, and the pawls let go. Let go and the springs push it back.
parts.moves: Up 4 mm when squeezed.

parts.label: Front plate
parts.what: The upright of the service drawer’s L: the pack’s face above the sill and the two columns, its round front corners and bands flush with the shell. A long finger pull along its foot and the charge strip along its top; nothing you carry by. The base plate is fixed to its foot.

parts.label: Base plate
parts.what: The floor of the service drawer’s L, riding on the shell’s foot between its two columns: every inner part is mounted on it, the film and the bottom plates, the cells’ holders, the clamp and the BMS. It runs on two low-friction strips on the foot’s top skin and slides out over the sill; the catches’ bolts click into the two notches in its edges.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of the face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge, one a tenth; the next one breathes while it charges, and when the BMS has opened the pack the lit ones blink red.
specs: State of charge, 10 % a segment; a fault in red
The BMS, by a ribbon up the face

parts.label: Clamp
parts.what: A stiff plate on four posts over the cells, its foam pad pressing every top contact plate onto its poles with about 90 N a cell: the only joining force in the pack, so every cell comes out again. On the drawer, so the cells stay pressed when it comes out.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic on the bottom contact plates with a socket for every cell’s foot: a floor with a hole under each cell for the plate’s spring finger, and a honeycomb of collars 6 mm high that keeps the cells 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate round the cells’ heads, its holes leaving each pole bare for the top contact plates.

parts.label: Insulation film
parts.what: A polyimide film between the bottom contact plates and the aluminium base plate: the plates are live, the drawer is not. Thin, so the cells’ heat still goes down through it into the drawer.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.source: Contact resistance of pressed copper busbars (J. Mech. Electr. Veh. 2019)
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells on the film: six that each join a row’s poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates, the pack’s minus (row 1) and plus (row 14). Each has a spring finger per cell, pressed up through the holder’s hole onto the pole by the clamp’s force: a pressed contact, no weld, so every cell comes out again.
specs: 0.15 A/mm² across a plate, 0.5 A/mm² in a finger at 100 A [computed]

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.source: Contact resistance of pressed copper busbars (J. Mech. Electr. Veh. 2019)
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s poles to the next row’s: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series, the current snaking up one row and down the next. Pressed flat onto the poles by the clamp’s pad.
specs: The clamp’s pad, ~90 N a cell

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board in front of the cells on the drawer: two front-end chips read every row’s voltage and the thermistors on the plates, a microcontroller runs the protection and talks CAN to the inverter through the plug. It opens the MOSFETs on any row under 2.80 V or over 4.25 V, any row over 60 °C, or over-current (past 100 A for 10 s, or 250 A at once), and bleeds the high rows at 100 mA above 4.10 V while charging so they stay together.
parts.moves: Opens and closes the pack.
specs: 2.8 V · 4.25 V · 60 °C · 100 A, 250 A for 10 s [inferred]

parts.label: MOSFET switches
parts.what: Sixteen power MOSFETs in two banks of eight on the board’s copper: one bank blocks discharge, the other charge, back to back in the pack’s minus line. They are the pack’s only switch: closed they drop a few millivolts, open the pack is dead at the plug.
parts.moves: Switch in microseconds.
specs: I²R: 5 W at 100 A, into the board’s copper

parts.label: Current shunt
parts.what: A manganin bar between two copper pads in the minus line: the BMS reads the pack’s current from the millivolts across it, for its counting of the charge and its over-current trip.

parts.label: Fuse
parts.what: A bolt-down fuse in the plus line, the last guard behind the MOSFETs: a dead short at the plug blows it before any strap or plate can heat.

parts.label: Balance leads
parts.what: Fifteen thin leads, one from every contact plate, so the BMS sees every row’s voltage and can bleed any row that runs ahead: from each plate’s end along the gap beside the holders, in front of the cells and up to the header on the board.

parts.label: Current straps
parts.what: Four flat copper straps in heat-shrink carry the pack’s current, each in the 3 mm gap between the holders and the shell’s wall: from row 14’s plate (the plus) up to the fuse, from the fuse down the right side and across the back to the plug’s plus; from the plug’s minus up the left side to the MOSFETs, and from the shunt along the right side, high, back to row 1’s plate (the minus). Bolted to the pads, no weld.
specs: 20 × 2 mm copper, 40 mm²: 2.5 A/mm² at 100 A [computed]
0.30 mΩ for the two long runs [computed]

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug whose two round pins and four data pins slide into the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home, into the same contact tubes the cube’s pins enter from the other side. Pull the drawer 10 mm and the pack is dead at its socket.
parts.moves: Leaves the socket with the drawer.
specs: The last 3.5 mm of the drawer’s travel

steps: Lay out the shell on its foot: floor tub, walls, top and back, its two corner columns with their release buttons and catches, the back socket, the grip and the ClickLock
Build the drawer: base plate and front plate with its finger pull and charge strip
Set the film, the bottom contact plates and the bottom holder on the base plate, and stand the 280 cells in it
Press on the top holder, the top plates and the clamp
Fit the BMS, its leads, the straps and the inner plug; slide the drawer in between the columns until both catches click into the base plate

assemblies.label: Shell
assemblies.note: The closed outer shell on its foot: floor tub, walls, top and back in one, open at the front above the foot’s sill. assemblies.label: Service drawer
assemblies.note: One L of aluminium riding on the shell’s foot: the front plate (the face above the sill and the two columns, with its finger pull and the charge strip) and the base plate behind it, running between the columns. It carries every inner part and nothing you hold: press the two buttons, pull it by its finger pull, and the whole inside comes out.

assemblies.label: Cells
assemblies.note: 280 cylindrical 21700 cells standing in two holder plates on the drawer, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side, every other row upside down so the plates alone join them.

assemblies.label: Contact plates
assemblies.note: Copper plates top and bottom that join each row to the next, pressed on by the drawer’s clamp, not welded: the bottom plates’ spring fingers reach the poles through the holder’s holes.

assemblies.label: BMS and plug
assemblies.note: The battery management system on the drawer (its MOSFETs, shunt, fuse and a balance lead to every row), the straps that carry the current, and its inner plug that meets the shell’s back socket when the drawer is in.

assemblies.label: ClickLock
assemblies.note: The snap-in latch that holds the pack in its cube, in the shell’s hollow foot: two spring pawls, their pivots and the cables to the grip’s trigger.

parts.label: Shell

parts.label: Back socket
parts.what: The pack’s plus, minus and data in one socket flush in its back, nothing sticking out, its holes in one line: guide, power, data, power, guide. The power contacts sit at the bottom of pockets that take the cube’s insulating collars, so no metal is ever open to a finger; the two lined guide holes take the cube’s guide pins first. Inside the wall the same contact tubes take the drawer’s inner plug: slide the pack in and it plugs itself into the backplane; pull the drawer and it lets go.
specs: 2 pockets ⌀ 19 mm, tubes for ⌀ 8 mm pins, 120 A [inferred]

parts.label: Grip

parts.label: Insulation film
parts.what: A polyimide film between the bottom contact plates and the aluminium base plate: the plates are live, the drawer is not. Thin, so the cells’ heat still goes down through it into the drawer.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.source: Contact resistance of pressed copper busbars (J. Mech. Electr. Veh. 2019)
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells on the film: six that each join a row’s poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates, the pack’s minus (row 1) and plus (row 14). Each has a spring finger per cell, pressed up through the holder’s hole onto the pole by the clamp’s force: a pressed contact, no weld, so every cell comes out again.
specs: 0.15 A/mm² across a plate, 0.5 A/mm² in a finger at 100 A [computed]

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.source: Contact resistance of pressed copper busbars (J. Mech. Electr. Veh. 2019)
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s poles to the next row’s: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series, the current snaking up one row and down the next. Pressed flat onto the poles by the clamp’s pad.
specs: The clamp’s pad, ~90 N a cell

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board in front of the cells on the drawer: two front-end chips read every row’s voltage and the thermistors on the plates, a microcontroller runs the protection and talks CAN to the inverter through the plug. It opens the MOSFETs on any row under 2.80 V or over 4.25 V, any row over 60 °C, or over-current (past 100 A for 10 s, or 250 A at once), and bleeds the high rows at 100 mA above 4.10 V while charging so they stay together.
parts.moves: Opens and closes the pack.
specs: 2.8 V · 4.25 V · 60 °C · 100 A, 250 A for 10 s [inferred]

parts.label: MOSFET switches
parts.what: Sixteen power MOSFETs in two banks of eight on the board’s copper: one bank blocks discharge, the other charge, back to back in the pack’s minus line. They are the pack’s only switch: closed they drop a few millivolts, open the pack is dead at the plug.
parts.moves: Switch in microseconds.
specs: I²R: 5 W at 100 A, into the board’s copper

parts.label: Current shunt
parts.what: A manganin bar between two copper pads in the minus line: the BMS reads the pack’s current from the millivolts across it, for its counting of the charge and its over-current trip.

parts.label: Fuse
parts.what: A bolt-down fuse in the plus line, the last guard behind the MOSFETs: a dead short at the plug blows it before any strap or plate can heat.

parts.label: Balance leads
parts.what: Fifteen thin leads, one from every contact plate, so the BMS sees every row’s voltage and can bleed any row that runs ahead: from each plate’s end along the gap beside the holders, in front of the cells and up to the header on the board.

parts.label: Current straps
parts.what: Four flat copper straps in heat-shrink carry the pack’s current, each in the 3 mm gap between the holders and the shell’s wall: from row 14’s plate (the plus) up to the fuse, from the fuse down the right side and across the back to the plug’s plus; from the plug’s minus up the left side to the MOSFETs, and from the shunt along the right side, high, back to row 1’s plate (the minus). Bolted to the pads, no weld.
specs: 20 × 2 mm copper, 40 mm²: 2.5 A/mm² at 100 A [computed]
0.30 mΩ for the two long runs [computed]

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug whose two round pins and four data pins slide into the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home, into the same contact tubes the cube’s pins enter from the other side. Pull the drawer 10 mm and the pack is dead at its socket.
parts.moves: Leaves the socket with the drawer.
specs: The last 3.5 mm of the drawer’s travel

steps: Lay out the shell on its foot: floor tub, walls, top and back, its two corner columns with their release buttons and catches, the back socket, the grip and the ClickLock
Build the drawer: base plate and front plate with its finger pull and charge strip
Set the film, the bottom contact plates and the bottom holder on the base plate, and stand the 280 cells in it
Press on the top holder, the top plates and the clamp
Fit the BMS, its leads, the straps and the inner plug; slide the drawer in between the columns until both catches click into the base plate

OCV against SoC of NMC cells (Chin. J. Mech. Eng. 31, 2018)

parts.label: Case
parts.what: The pack’s case: one smooth aluminium shell with round corners, its floor and four walls, a darker foot band, and rails under it to slide on.

parts.label: Front panel
parts.what: The pack’s face, set into the case’s front: it carries the handles, the charge strip along its top and the terminals.

parts.label: Charge strip
parts.what: A slim LED strip along the top of its face, under the lid’s seam: ten segments light up with the pack’s state of charge.

parts.label: Handles
parts.what: Two handles on its face to slide it in and out: at ~26 kg one person lifts it.

parts.label: Bottom contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates under the cells, each joining a row’s minus poles to the next row’s, and the two end plates that go to the terminals.

parts.label: Bottom cell holder
parts.what: A plate of flame-retardant plastic with a socket for every cell’s foot: it keeps them 22 mm apart, air between them.

parts.label: 21700 cells
parts.what: Cylindrical lithium-ion cells, 21 mm across and 70 mm high, 14 rows in series of 20 side by side. Each is held, not welded: a worn cell is pulled and a new one pushed in.

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Terminals
parts.what: The pack’s plus and minus on its face, under their covers, and the data plug for the BMS beside them.

parts.label: Lid
parts.what: The lid, its round corners and soft edge flush with the case, and the spring pad under it: closing it presses every contact plate onto its poles, the whole pack’s only joining force.

parts.label: Latches
parts.what: Four flush over-centre latches, two a side: flip them and the lid lifts. No tool opens the pack.

steps: Lay out the tray, its front panel, handles and ClickLock
Set the bottom contact plates and holder, and stand the 280 cells in it
Press on the top holder and the top contact plates
Fit the BMS, its sense leads and the back plug
Close the lid on its spring pad and snap the four latches

parts.label: Top cell holder
parts.what: The same plate over the cells’ heads, its openings leaving each pole bare for the contact plates.

parts.label: Top contact plates
parts.what: Copper plates over the cells, each joining a row’s plus poles to the next row’s minus: with the bottom plates they put the 14 rows in series.

parts.label: Battery management system
parts.what: The board behind the cells: a lead to each of the 14 rows, it balances them, keeps them within their voltage and temperature, and opens the pack if anything goes wrong.

parts.label: Back socket
parts.what: The pack’s plus, minus and data in one socket flush in its back, nothing sticking out. Its contacts sit at the bottom of pockets that take the cube’s insulating collars: the collars slide in first, then the pins meet their contacts, so no metal is ever open to a finger on either side. Two lined guide holes take the cube’s guide pins first: slide the pack in and it plugs itself into the backplane; pull it out and it lets go.
specs: 2 pockets ⌀ 19 mm, sockets for ⌀ 8 mm pins, 120 A [inferred]
2 lined holes, ⌀ 11 mm, for ⌀ 10 mm pins

parts.label: Pawls
parts.what: Two steel levers, one inside each side wall. Each pivots at its back end; its tooth at the front pokes out through a slot in the wall. Sliding in, the tooth rides up the rail’s ramp, is pushed in, and snaps out again behind the keeper: that is the click.

parts.label: Pawl springs
parts.what: A small coil spring behind each pawl presses its tooth outward, so it always drops into the keeper on its own: you never have to lock it, only to unlock it.

parts.label: Pivot pins
parts.what: A pin through each pawl’s back end, standing in the case floor: the pawl swings round it, in and out.

parts.label: Release cables
parts.what: Two short steel cables in sleeves, both at the pawls’ own height: from the trigger in through the face, along its inside to the corner and straight back along the side wall to the pawl, no bend up or down. Pulling the trigger pulls both cables, and both pawls swing in together, out of their keepers.
specs: ⌀ 1.5 mm steel in a PTFE sleeve

parts.label: Trigger
parts.what: The bar under the grip: your fingers close round the grip and press it up, it pulls both cables, and the pawls let go. Let go and the springs push it back.

parts.label: Clamp
parts.what: A stiff plate on four posts over the cells, its spring pad pressing every top contact plate onto its poles: the job the lid did, now on the drawer, so the cells stay pressed when it comes out.

parts.label: Inner plug
parts.what: At the back of the drawer: the BMS’s plus, minus and data in one plug that slides onto the inside of the shell’s back socket as the drawer goes home.

parts.label: Release button, left
parts.what: A round push button in the face of the shell’s corner column on its side, at the base plate’s level: part of the shell, so it stays put while the drawer comes out. Behind it a short plunger with a wedge runs back inside the column and pushes the catch’s bolt out of its notch in the base plate. Press both, pull the drawer by its finger pull, and the whole inside slides out between the columns.

parts.label: Drawer catch, left
parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.

parts.label: Release button, right
parts.what: A round push button in the face of the shell’s corner column on its side, at the base plate’s level: part of the shell, so it stays put while the drawer comes out. Behind it a short plunger with a wedge runs back inside the column and pushes the catch’s bolt out of its notch in the base plate. Press both, pull the drawer by its finger pull, and the whole inside slides out between the columns.

parts.label: Drawer catch, right
parts.what: A spring bolt lying across inside the shell’s corner column, at the base plate’s height: its spring pushes its tip into a notch in the base plate’s edge and holds the drawer in. The button’s wedge pushes it back out; slide the drawer home and the bolt clicks in again on its own.

steps: Lay out the shell on its foot: floor tub, walls, top and back, its two corner columns with their release buttons and catches, the back socket, the grip and the ClickLock
Build the drawer: base plate and front plate with its finger pull and charge strip
Set the bottom contact plates and holder on the base plate, and stand the 280 cells in it
Press on the top holder, the top plates and the clamp
Fit the BMS, its leads and the inner plug; slide the drawer in between the columns until both catches click into the base plate

f14492aa9c71a4d51852aee9460d47727b15d258.label: ElectroCube: ElectroCube
f14492aa9c71a4d51852aee9460d47727b15d258.note: as at v1: a classic alternator, 35" (0.9 m) long

assemblies.label: Frame
assemblies.note: A 27" cube: two 4×4 tube skids carry everything and take the lifting pins; 2×2 angle posts and top rails close it, and its quick-attach plate couples it to a machine.

assemblies.label: Engine
assemblies.note: A 28 hp Briggs & Stratton air-cooled V-twin with electric start, on its mount plate: the prime mover of every machine the cube is coupled to.

assemblies.label: Electrics
assemblies.note: A brushless alternator flanged to the engine and turned by its shaft, its voltage regulator and breakers in a box on the back, and the sockets a home, a workshop or the village grid plugs into.

assemblies.label: Fuel and controls
assemblies.note: The removable 7-gallon fuel tank, the 12 V battery and the panel with the key, the choke and the throttle.

parts.label: Power Cube base skids (4×4 tube)
parts.what: Two 4×4 steel tubes front to back under the cube: the “strong structural frame” of 7s that the engine, pump and tanks bolt to, and that takes the forks, the lifting pins or another cube stacked on it.

parts.label: Power Cube posts and top rails (2×2 angle)
parts.what: Four corner posts and four top rails of 1/4" × 2" × 2" angle make the cube’s cage: they guard the engine, carry the fuel tank and give hand-holds to lift it by. OSE’s frame page cuts its members 29", 27" and 24" long.

parts.label: Power Cube quick-attach plate
parts.what: How the cube is coupled to a machine: plates across its back with a 4×8 receiver tube between them, so it slides onto the machine’s mount and is pinned, and comes off again in minutes for the next machine. Several cubes can be strung together for more power.

parts.label: Power Cube lifting eyes
parts.what: Two eyes on the top rails: at about 181 kg the cube is lifted on and off a machine by the loader, a hoist or two people with a bar.

parts.label: Engine mount plate
parts.what: The plate the engine’s base bolts to, itself bolted across the skids: it holds the engine’s shaft exactly in line with the pump’s.

parts.label: Engine crankcase
parts.what: The 28 hp Briggs & Stratton V-twin’s crankcase: crankshaft, camshaft, the oil sump and the governor that holds it at its speed. The crankshaft runs fore and aft: the flywheel at the front, the pump at the back.
parts.moves: The crankshaft inside turns at engine speed.
specs: Briggs & Stratton 28 hp (20.9 kW) V-twin, air-cooled

parts.label: Engine cylinder and head, left
parts.what: One bank of the 90° V-twin: a finned air-cooled cylinder and its overhead-valve head. The flywheel’s fan pushes air through the shroud and over these fins.
parts.moves: Its piston runs up and down inside, twice per two turns of the crank.

parts.label: Engine cylinder and head, right
parts.what: One bank of the 90° V-twin: a finned air-cooled cylinder and its overhead-valve head. The flywheel’s fan pushes air through the shroud and over these fins.
parts.moves: Its piston runs up and down inside, twice per two turns of the crank.

parts.label: Blower housing
parts.what: The shroud over the flywheel, ducting its fan’s air back over both cylinders.

parts.label: Flywheel and fan screen
parts.what: The flywheel at the crank’s front: its weight smooths the twin’s firing, its magnets fire the plugs and charge the battery, its vanes are the cooling fan.
parts.moves: Turns with the crankshaft (shown slowed: really 60 turns a second).

parts.label: Air cleaner
parts.what: The paper element in the V between the cylinders: every litre of air the engine breathes is cleaned here first.

parts.label: Muffler
parts.what: The Briggs & Stratton muffler behind the cylinders, collecting both exhausts into one can and blowing out to the side.

parts.label: Electric starter
parts.what: The 12 V starter whose pinion meshes with the flywheel’s ring gear while the key is held to START.
parts.moves: Spins only while starting.

parts.label: Flexible coupling
parts.what: A rubber-element coupling between the engine’s shaft and the alternator’s rotor: it takes up the twin’s firing pulses so the rotor turns smoothly.
parts.moves: Turns with the engine (shown slowed).
parts.drive: The crankshaft; it drives the rotor

parts.label: Alternator adapter (bell housing)
parts.what: An SAE bell housing bolted to the engine’s face and the alternator’s flange: it holds the two shafts in line, as the pump mount did.

parts.label: Brushless alternator
parts.what: A single-bearing, brushless synchronous alternator: its rotor turns inside the stator’s copper windings and gives alternating current at the engine’s governed speed. The 28 hp twin carries about 15 kVA of it.
parts.moves: Its rotor turns with the engine.
specs: 400 V three-phase and 230 V, 50 Hz at 3,000 rpm (60 Hz at 3,600)
Its own fan, on the rotor

parts.label: Alternator foot
parts.what: A steel foot under the alternator’s end bell, bolted to the frame’s back cross member on rubber mounts; its flange end hangs on the engine.

parts.label: Control box (regulator and breakers)
parts.what: The box on the cube’s back: the automatic voltage regulator that holds the voltage steady as loads come and go, the main breaker, an earth-leakage breaker, an hour meter and a voltmeter.

parts.label: Sockets
parts.what: What the cube gives out: a red three-phase socket for the village grid or a workshop, and two blue 230 V sockets for a home or tools, each under its spring lid.

parts.label: Alternator cable
parts.what: The armoured cable from the alternator’s terminal box to the control box and sockets.

parts.label: Fuel tank (7 gal)
parts.what: The removable petrol tank on top of the cube, over the engine: lift it off to fill it away from the machine.

parts.label: 12 V battery
parts.what: The cube’s own 12 V battery beside the engine: it cranks the starter, runs the cooler fan and the machine’s valves; the flywheel alternator charges it.

parts.label: Control panel
parts.what: On the front corner post: the key switch (off, run, start), the choke and the throttle. The cube is started here and left running; the machine’s valves do the rest.
parts.moves: Key, choke and throttle are worked by hand.

steps: Cut, drill and bolt the frame: skids, posts, top rails, quick-attach plate
Bolt in the engine on its mount plate
Flange the alternator to the engine on its coupling; fit its feet, the control box, the sockets and the cable
Fit the fuel tank, the battery and the control panel
